rv.q: Bloom is so good in her default mode, with a glint in her eye and dozens of curse words in her mouth, that she wins you over to her helter-skelter view of the world.

More than blunt language — a tool that loses its sharpness with use — this absurdist vein effectively draws laughs, but it also underscores the show's real subject: the often cruel arbitrariness of life.
I can think of few more delightful, hilariously tuneful ways.
Bloom uses this mawkish fantasy to tie her shambolic musings into one neat, colorful, hilarious bow.
She's holding space for us to work through it with humor and heart. Sometimes that's good enough.
The show instead leaves the impression that Bloom is rushing to process grief, joy, and the last decade of her career before the pop culture moment moves on.
Maybe it is occasionally humorous, but it's got nothing to do with wit.
Its quickly-paced ninety minutes flew by and once out in the street, audience members like me were still laughing.
Bloom is a witty narrator of her journey, quick on her feet with a timely ad-lib
